name: Yusuf Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What fills an ordinary day on your crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a distribution crew on city streets, from failed transformers behind shops to cable faults in damp vaults. My two-year technical diploma helps with the diagrams; thirty years of work helps when the diagram is wrong. I still like hearing a whole block come back to life.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Night callouts, mostly, and traffic around the repair truck. My wife Leila works nursing shifts, and our grown daughter Samira is learning the line trade on her own wage. I use an AI drafting tool now and then, after someone has shown it works, but I read every order myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the yard that a little help with the outage list is welcome, but the wires still need us. The little AI drafting tool I use now and then would be enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila, my wife, has her nursing shifts, and we have savings beyond six months. I earn well leading the distribution crew and could probably finish my last working years here, even with the ordinary worry of night callouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the city fault rota and checking every isolation order against the site. I would also keep attending the monthly safety committee meeting, as I already do, and bring the crew’s near misses to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My shoulders may be older than the cables, but the household money is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which near miss would you bring this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A traffic barrier was moved before we had finished at a street vault. I would ask the committee to mark who may clear the barriers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you increase your AI use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a modest tool. I use it for an occasional wording problem, then read the order myself before the crew moves.

say: I would welcome modest **outage-list help** while reminding the yard that field repairs still need people.
I would tell colleagues the occasional **drafting tool** is enough for my present work.
think: Our **strong savings** and Leila’s nursing shifts leave my last working years financially steady.
The night rota still takes a **physical toll**, even if the AI change is small.
do: Keep the **city fault rota** and check isolation orders on site.
Continue the existing **safety committee** attendance and report the traffic barrier near miss.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, with some weariness about night callouts.
S0.quote: My shoulders may be older than the cables, but the household money is steady.
fieldNote: He has high pay, a second wage and **strong savings**, supporting a calm baseline.
His AI use and safety committee work are both **existing habits**, so the action remains continuation.

steps.text: Keep leading city fault repairs and checking isolation orders on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that software can do the booking and buying, but a crew should sign off a route before it touches a live street. I would take a proposed rule to the safety committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planners could lose posts and my daughter Samira, a line apprentice, may see fewer places after qualification. My own field wage looks secure for the next few years, though I would watch whether the company starts trimming night overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the safety committee to require a named lineworker on every AI dispatch plan. If the depot offers its new routing screen after a field trial, I would learn how to check its alerts with a younger dispatcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the people around me, not frightened about my own pay. Samira has time to build skills, but fewer posts would hurt. Samira, my daughter, should not have to guess which line jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the routing screen worth learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A field trial that catches bad access notes instead of merely making a tidy map. I would want the dispatcher to show me the alert history on two actual faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Samira live on your income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she has her own apprenticeship wage. Leila and I can help with a course if she asks, but I am not assuming she will lose that job.

say: I would seek a **named lineworker** to sign off AI dispatch plans near live streets.
I would raise the rule at the next **safety committee** meeting.
think: My **own wage** looks secure, but planners and newly qualified apprentices face a changing market.
Samira has her own **apprentice pay**, so her uncertainty is a concern rather than a household wage loss.
do: Propose a **dispatch sign-off rule** at the next safety committee meeting.
Learn the new **routing alerts** with a dispatcher only after a field trial proves useful.
feel: **Uneasy** for planners and apprentices while my own income appears secure.
S1.quote: Samira, my daughter, should not have to guess which line jobs remain.
fieldNote: His concern for Samira is genuine, but her separate wage does not create **household income risk**.
He would learn new routing alerts only after a **proven field trial**, consistent with steady adaptability.

steps.text: Propose named lineworker dispatch sign-off at the next safety committee meeting
Learn new AI routing alerts with a dispatcher after a useful field trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a thinking system in 2028 can plan a repair but cannot clear a burnt transformer. By 2031, when capable robots arrive, I would want trial results from our own streets before any crew is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to work several years beyond 2031 if my health holds. The company might shrink the fault crews when robots can do the hands-on work; savings and nearby utilities give us room, but a lower wage would change our retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union branch for paid field trials and a published crew staffing plan. If the company cuts my shifts for two rosters, I would apply to nearby utilities before drawing on savings; I would keep my present job until a firm offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours for the first time in these pictures. I can make a move, but I cannot make a robot trial safe by wishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at the first cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need a firm offer with comparable pay before leaving the depot, and Leila and I would check the household numbers together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the field trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot handling a wet vault and a damaged transformer without hiding its errors. I want the crew to be able to stop a trial immediately.

say: I would demand local **2031 robot trials** before fault crews are cut.
I would ask the **union branch** for published staffing plans and paid crew involvement.
think: I expect to need my **field wage** beyond 2031, when robots could reduce fault shifts.
Savings and nearby jobs give options, but a **lower wage** would change retirement arithmetic.
do: Join the **union branch** push for paid trials and a crew staffing plan.
Apply to **nearby utilities** after two reduced rosters, leaving only for a comparable firm offer.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic cut to my own field hours, with alternatives available.
S2.quote: I cannot make a robot trial safe by wishing.
fieldNote: He distinguishes the earlier **thinking date** from the later hands-on robot risk.
The job search is tied to **two reduced rosters** and any departure to comparable firm pay.

steps.text: Join union push for paid robot trials and a published staffing plan
Apply to nearby utilities after two reduced rosters and leave only for comparable firm pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that the extra years permit proper testing in bad weather, not just a showroom. A robot doing repairs around 2034 should have to meet the checks we give a new worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty six when robots arrive, I may already have left regular climbing if our health and accounts allow. Thinking AI in 2031 would alter paperwork first, and I can check a generated order without giving it my judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the fault crew next year and teach the younger lead how I isolate a vault. Leila and I would review our retirement accounts each autumn, then choose the date on the figures rather than the robot calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about next year’s wage, though I still think about who trains the next lead. A few years make the transition less abrupt for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire earlier in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might, but I would not promise an earlier date until Leila and I know what her shifts and our expenses look like. Our retirement review is not a resignation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can a new lead learn in the vault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to stop when the drawing and the cable tags disagree. I would have them point to every isolation point before anyone enters.

say: I would demand **bad-weather testing** before 2034 robots repair city lines.
I would teach the next **crew lead** to verify vault isolation in person.
think: I may leave regular climbing before **2034**, conditional on health and household accounts.
The **2031 paperwork** change is manageable while my field judgement remains useful.
do: Keep leading **fault repairs** and teach the younger lead vault isolation.
Review **retirement accounts** with Leila each autumn before choosing a date.
feel: **Calm** about my near-term wage, with concern for the next lead’s training.
S3.quote: Our retirement review is not a resignation.
fieldNote: He separates a possible future retirement from any actual **early-exit action** in this scenario.
His strong cushion supports confidence, while **health and accounts** still govern the date.

steps.text: Keep leading city fault repairs and teaching the younger lead vault isolation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the safety committee a decade is enough to write rules with lineworkers at the table. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 should not decide who takes responsibility for a live repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to be retired before 2036 if health and our savings hold up. Leila and I still have to set the exact date, but a robot arriving in 2039 is unlikely to touch my own pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work the usual rota this year and bring a written human sign-off proposal to the next safety committee meeting. I would ask the union to keep apprentice training in the proposal, because younger workers have a longer stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for myself and still engaged for the trade. The decade gives us room to get the rule right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should sign a robot repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trained lineworker who has checked the isolation and the repair record. The company can choose the machine, but it cannot send accountability into a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will the card change your retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Leila and I will pick that from health, savings and her work plans, just as we would without the card.

say: I would call for **worker-written rules** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots reach live repairs.
I would include **apprentice training** in the safety committee proposal.
think: I expect to retire before **2036** if health and savings follow our plan.
The **2039 robot date** seems too late to threaten my own wage.
do: Keep the **usual fault rota** for this first year.
Bring a written **human sign-off proposal** to the next safety committee meeting.
feel: **Calm** about my own income, engaged with the future of the trade.
S4.quote: The company can choose the machine, but it cannot send accountability into a box.
fieldNote: His own retirement remains conditional on **health and savings**, not moved forward by this card.
He uses an existing group to advance a **new specific rule** for robot repairs.

steps.text: Keep leading the usual city fault rota
Bring human sign-off and apprentice training proposal to the safety committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the 2031 robots could cut my own fault shifts before I finish working. Paid trials with our crew, a published staffing plan and clear human sign-off would let me plan with Leila rather than guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the younger crew when old hands leave. A company cannot train a lineworker by showing a robot video at the depot.

headlineQuote: A company cannot train a lineworker by showing a robot video at the depot.
portrait: **Yusuf**, 58, is a highly skilled city distribution lead with a technical diploma, higher pay and more than six months saved.
His wife earns from **nursing**, and plenty of nearby utilities give him options if field hours fall.
He uses **AI occasionally** after seeing proof and brings new safety proposals through his union and committee.
The **2028 case** worries him most because robots could reach his fault work in 2031 before he retires.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his fault shifts when capable robots reach the field in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid field trials**, published staffing and human sign-off would help him plan with Leila.
